title: Beyond Bandwidth: The Practical Advantages of Dedicated Optical Wave Service
summary: Cogent is one of the world's largest Internet Service Providers, delivering high-quality Internet, Ethernet and Colocation services.
body_markdown:
*November 15 2026 byClaude West*


[From jumbo frames to network transparency, understanding what dedicated optical transport means for your WAN](https://www.cogentco.com/cogent-blog/5152-beyond-bandwidth-the-practical-advantages-of-dedicated-optical-wave-service)


[Read on for more](https://www.cogentco.com/cogent-blog/5152-beyond-bandwidth-the-practical-advantages-of-dedicated-optical-wave-service)


When network engineers evaluate connectivity between two data centers, bandwidth is often the first consideration. But bandwidth is only part of the equation. What happens to your traffic between those locations? How much control do you keep? And how does the architecture affect performance, security, and resiliency?


In my previous article,[The Network Behind the Workload: Why Optical Waves Matter in the AI Era](https://www.cogentco.com/cogent-blog/5143-the-network-behind-the-workload-why-optical-waves-matter-in-the-ai-era) , I covered why optical transport matters for AI and cloud. This time, let's look at the technology's practical advantages.


**1. Simplicity: Your Network, Our Transport**


Imagine two data centers, one in Dallas and one in Chicago, each with a router supporting a 100G wave interface. Between them, the signal may cross hundreds of miles of fiber, amplifiers, and ROADMs. That's the complicated part, and the provider handles it.


The customer gets a familiar 100GE ethernet interface and controls what runs across it.


**The advantage:** A long-distance, high-capacity connection that operates like a direct link between your own devices.


**2. Frame Size: Why End-to-End Transparency Matters**


Most engineers know Ethernet's common 1,500-byte MTU. Many modern devices also support 9,000-byte jumbo frames.


Take an 80-gigabyte dataset, using a simplified calculation based on payload size:


**Payload size**


**Approximate** **# of frames**


1,500 bytes


53.3 million


9,000 bytes


8.9 million


That's about 83% fewer packets to process, which can reduce overhead depending on your hardware and applications.


But what about the network between the endpoints? With a managed Layer 2 Ethernet service, the provider must engineer every packet-forwarding component to carry your frame size. If one can't, it may drop oversized frames, even when both ends are configured correctly.


A transparent wavelength carries the provisioned client signal without making forwarding decisions on individual frames. Cogent's Ethernet LAN-PHY wavelength handoffs support frames up to 9,600 bytes, enough for common 9,000-byte jumbo configurations. OTU handoffs impose no Ethernet frame-size limitation, so customers operate according to their own equipment and the applicable OTN interface specifications.


While Ethernet Private Line and VPLS services can support jumbo frames too, a wavelength avoids the intermediate packet-switching dependencies.


**The advantage:** Frame sizes optimized around your applications and equipment, without carrier MTU constraints.


**3. Security: Understanding the Layer 1 Advantage**


IP routing operates at Layer 3 and Ethernet switching at Layer 2. A dedicated wavelength provides transport at Layer 1.


The optical network makes no routing or switching decisions based on your packets, and no customer routing or MAC tables sit in the path. That separates your traffic from the provider's shared packet-forwarding environment and reduces exposure to certain packet-layer vulnerabilities. In most cases, Cogent separates the physical layer of the IP and wavelength core, end to end.


It doesn't make a wavelength impossible to intercept, and sensitive data still needs encryption and other controls. But the distinction matters. The Internet relies on optical transport, dedicated wavelengths don’t use the public internet.


**4. Dedicated Capacity: Predictable Performance by Design**


A 100G wavelength gives the customer 100G of provisioned capacity between two endpoints. You aren't competing with other subscribers for it, and no intermediate routers or switches add packet queuing. Fiber distance, fiber characteristics, and the optical equipment's processing characteristics drive latency.


For financial market data, distributed storage, and other latency-sensitive applications, consistent performance can matter as much as bandwidth. MPLS and Ethernet services can also perform well with capacity engineering and QoS. The wavelength advantage is architectural simplicity.


**The advantage:** Dedicated bandwidth and predictable point-to-point performance.


**5. Physical Paths: Knowing Where Your Traffic Travels**


Say you connect two data centers with redundant 100G circuits from different providers. If both run through the same conduit or bridge crossing, a single fiber cut could disrupt both.


Engineered wavelength services let customers evaluate KMZ route files, fiber mileage, round-trip delay, and route diversity, so engineers can spot shared-risk infrastructure. Two wavelengths between Dallas and Chicago could run over geographically diverse routes.


MPLS, EPL, and VPLS provide resilient designs differently from wavelengths. Their underlying layer 3 routing, or “switched fabric” architecture, allow for failover when congestion or outages occur. Restoration, protection, and maintenance can still affect routing, and there is no guarantee regarding the physical path between endpoints.


**The advantage:** Resiliency designed around documented physical routes, not logical topology alone.


**6. The Right Technology for the Right Application**


Wavelengths don't replace every WAN service. Ethernet Private Line offers managed point-to-point Layer 2 connectivity. VPLS extends Ethernet across multiple sites. MPLS IP-VPN provides managed Layer 3 connectivity for multisite WANs.


These technologies complement one another. A large enterprise might use MPLS across dozens of locations, VPLS for multipoint Ethernet needs, and 100G or 400G wavelengths between its primary data centers.


***The goal is to match the connectivity architecture to the application.***
